newsitem.title: USA: U.S. brokers spend heavily on 2000 computer bug.
newsitem.headline: U.S. brokers spend heavily on 2000 computer bug.

text.p: U.S. brokers and investment banks are spending heavily to make sure their computer systems will not crash in 2000, an industry group said on Tuesday.

The Securities Industry Association (SIA), in a study conducted with the Tower Group, found that millennium projects and broker workstation development ranked as the first or second-largest technology development project at most firms.

The industry invested $11.5 billion in information technology in 1996, the study found. Firms allocated an average of 63 percent of their budgets to technology to avoid problems in 2000 and other maintenance projects.

"The year 2000 project is estimated to consume 5,048 person-years and billions of dollars industrywide between now and January 1, 2000," Diogo Teixeira, president of Tower Group said in a statement. "The industry is committing these resources to ensure that the systems remain operational after New Year's Day."
Numerous experts have warned that computer systems using two digits to express the date may malfunction unless modified before the new millennium.

The study also found firms busy working on development projects including creation of new financial products, streamlining transactions, enhancing risk management systems and expanding use of the Internet and Intranets.

"Firms invested heavily in technology to improve communications with customers and distribute information within and outside the firms," Marc Lackritz, president of the SIA said in a statement. "Three percent of the securities industry's IT (informaton technology) budget was spent on Internet/Intranet/Extranet development alone."
The study found that firms are using Intranet and Extranet technology to expand access to research reports and market data internally. Some firms are expanding the access to clients.
The number of company websites is expected to grow at a compund annual rate of 50 percent with virtually every firm planning to have at least one website by 2000, the study said.

Those surveyed planned continued growth in Internet spending, projecting annual budgets in 2000 to be between $875 million and $1.3 billion. The estimated range of spending in 2000 would represent an annual compound growth rate ranging between 39 percent and 54 percent, the SIA said.
